classrooms. Nearly 300 principals will get the opportunity to mentor and grow the
strength of our 2,500 principals  across the country. That is  how much members on this
side of the House care about ed ucation. We have grown the i nvestment in it every year
at every level of education because we know that that is the bi ggest contribution you
can make to a young person—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: Last week I advised th e House that the recent
US National Climate Assessment report descri bed climate change as no longer a distant
threat but a clear and present danger, and th at that report was a corroboration of the
Global Assessment Report by the United Nations a few months earlier. So we now have
it officially on record that climate change is a present threat to humankind. I do not
think it is possible to understa te the magnitude of the threat  we are facing. It is a clear
and present danger in the form of the extrem e weather events we have been witnessing
these past few years. On the strength of a 0.8 degree temperature rise, we are witnessing
the likes of hurricanes Katrina and Sandy in the United States and Haiyan in the
Philippines, along with floods in Asia and the Americas, forest fires in Russia and
Australia, and heatwaves and droughts in Europe and elsewhere, including here.
The long-term danger is greater still. Three scientific studies re cently released give
testimony to this. A report by National Ae ronautics and Space Administration and the
University of California finds that six majo r glaciers in West Antarctica seem to be
locked in an irreversible thaw linked to global warming. Six glaciers eaten away from
below by the warming waters round the ice continent are flowing fast into the
Amundsen Sea, according to satellite data fo r the past two decades. According to the
lead author, a large sector of the West Antarctic ice sh eet has gone into “a state of
irreversible retreat”. The gl aciers hold enough ice to raise sea levels by 1.2 metres over
a period of centuries. According to the lead  author, this has “p assed the point of no
return”. A separate study by the University  of Washington focuses on one of these
glaciers. The Thwaites Glacier acts as a linc hpin on the rest of the West Antarctic ice
sheet, which contains enough ice to cause another 3 to 4 metres of sea level rise.
A third study, by the Potsdam Institute fo r Climate Impact Research, conveys new
findings on East Antarctica, wh ich contains 10 times more ice than West Antarctica.
According to the head of Potsdam’s global adaptation strategies project: “Until recently,
only West Antarctica was considered unstable,  but now we know that its … counterpart
in the East might also be at risk. … We have probably overestimated the stability of
East Antarctica so far.” If half of the so-called ice cork were to melt, the discharge
would begin and could lead to a sea level rise of another 3 to 4 metres over the long
term.
Of course, the United Nations’ Fifth A ssessment Report stretches out just one
century, to 2100. Its 100-year scenario is of a rise by 0.26 to 0.82 metres, but scientists
have known that ice melt in Antarctica will occur over centuries and as far out as 1,000
years. This raises the question: how far out should humanity be concerned as a result of
the consequence of its own actions? I suggest indefinite ly—as far out as the human
14 May 2014 General Debate 17837
mind can contemplate—because we temporary custodians today have no right to set a
sunset clause on the human future. I invite  my National colleagues in the Chamber to
read from their script that this is alarmist nonsense. They are the same MPs who failed
to turn up to the parliamentary briefing our Kiwi  scientists gave on these issues just last
October.
To the extent that such ice melt is irrevers ible, we must begin to learn to adapt. But
above all we must up our game on mitiga tion, reducing emissions—very far and very
fast. Why should we care today about future generations? For those who have to ask the
question, there is a ready and e qually self-interested answer. It is because the clear and
present danger applies to New Zealand’s wa y of life. It puts today’s economy, today’s
jobs, the homes we live in today, and the lo cal environment we enjoy today at risk—
today. This Government’s policies are making things worse and putting New Zealand at
risk through its inaction—today. The Gr een Party is moving, as we enter the
forthcoming election campaign, to make climate protection one of our highest priorities.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Very little of  what has gone
on in this Chamber in the last week or so would have had any connection with New
Zealanders, who would genera lly be reviled by the mud-s linging, the abuse, the name-
calling, and all of the vituperation and retribution that seem to have become the stock in
trade of parliamentary debate in recent times. Perhaps it is forgivable in the smallest
extent by the pending election, but it is not justifiable nor is it appreciated by the bulk of
New Zealanders.
For most New Zealanders the challenge is a very simple one. This country has come
out of the worst economic crisis since the Gr eat Depression—the global financial crisis.
We have been through 5 or 6 ve ry difficult, tough years, wh ere the Minister of Finance
and the Government have shown considerable discipline in terms of both their spending
policies and the direction of overall economic  policies. Now, instead of name-calling
and catcalling and rumour-mongering, what New Zealanders are looking forward to is a
dividend on the investment they made in  2008 and 2011 when they elected this
Government to office. They expect to see in tomorrow’s Budget some signs of progress
for the future, of steps that give them confid ence in the decisions they have to make in
their lives to give opportunity and the prospect of hope to their children.
One area I want to talk about, which I think is very critical to the future of this
country, is tertiary education. I think it is time to take a more radical approach to the
issue of funding tertiary edu cation. The current system of a fees-based system paid by
the contributor, the student, supplemented in some cases, but by no means all, by a
system of student allowances a nd student loans, has, I think,  had its day. The fact that
we have large student loan indebtedness and we are doing all we ca n, quite properly, to
recover that debt suggests that a continuati on of the same sort of policy is simply a
repetition of what we have done previously.
Maybe the way forward is to turn the system on its head, to abolish student
allowances completely—because not all students are currently eligible—and to use the
money thus saved to reduce, and if not reduce then eliminate, the tertiary fees that they
pay. So you would get a system, with some modest additional investment from the
Government, of tertiary educa tion returning to essentially being free to the user. But
students are then responsible for their living costs and their course costs throughout, and
that will be where the loan system, in a much more disciplined way, could take some
effect. Carrying on the way we are will si mply produce more indebtedness and more
problems for people trying to recover from th at indebtedness and trying to make a long-
term contribution to New Zealand.
There is another area I think is worth considering. For many New Zealanders the
option of tertiary education simply is not th ere, because there is no family history of a
17838 General Debate 14 May 2014
tertiary education. The family does not have that in their, if you like, set of horizons
about what their children might do. I think th ere is scope for considering some form of
incentive to enable first-time entrants from families who have not previously been in the
tertiary education system to come in and to  benefit. That is the way you broaden the
basis of the system. That is the way you give  access to those who may well be currently
excluded, but it is also the way you make it cl ear that tertiary education is not the
preserve of the elite but an opportunity for a ll to participate. As a consequence, not only
do you broaden the base of education and ach ievement and the ability for people to
make a contribution to our so ciety that is posi tive and long term but you encourage
future generations as well.
When we start to think about the steps forward that I hope this Budget tomorrow will
indicate, in terms of our having turned the ec onomic corner, then it is important to start
to think about how we utilise the fruits of those long-term gains to the benefit of the
people whom we are elected to serve. I say one  thing as I close: the expectation of New
Zealanders is that we contribute positively. It is not that we carry on in the way that this
House has been doing in recent times. I think we have reached new lows, and the danger
is that there is an even lower floor to be set if we continue as we are. Tomorrow
provides an opportunity to move forward with  some optimism. I hope that the Minister
and the Government take it and that Parliament responds accordingly.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: The Prime Minister
stood up in the House today and, as he often does, told us of the terrible things he
inherited from the Labour Government. They  were terrible thin gs like the lowest
unemployment rate in the OECD and zero net debt—shocking things that cause so
much difficulty for the National Government . The Prime Minister is fond of talking
about people’s horses. Well, John Key’ s horse of hypocrisy is tied up at “Debt
Mountain”, where he has borro wed $57.7 billion since he came  into Government. That
is nearly $60 billion borrowed by this Government.
We on this side of the House will not take being lectured by that side of the House
about who is a good fiscal manager, a bout who is delivering on the economy. The
Labour Party is proud that on average for 5 years we held unemployment under 4
percent, and we will do it again. We will be a Government that puts people at the centre
of the economy. Not speculators, not big interests, not the wealthy few, not the mates of
Ministers, but ordinary, ev eryday New Zealanders will be  given a chance and an
opportunity.
Tomorrow the Government has the opportunity to deliver to New Zealanders. It has
the opportunity to deliver to 147,000 New Zealanders who are out of work and want a
job. It has got the opportunity to deliver to the 46 percent of salary and wage earners
who did not get a pay rise last year while th e bosses at the top end did. It has got an
opportunity to deliver to the 285,000 children who live in poverty in New Zealand. That
is a figure that the Prime Minister tried to deny today. He tried to not take responsibility
for it. He could deliver for them tomorrow.  He could deliver fo r the 40,000 children
hospitalised with skin infections and respiratory illnesses caused by the cold, damp
homes they live in. He coul d deliver for them tomorrow. He could deliver for the
thousands of first-home buyers who have missed out on getting on to the property
ladder under his Government—but he will not.
He will not deliver for them, because tomo rrow will be Bill English’s sixth big let-
down. It will be the sixth time that the wealthy few get prioritised over the ordinary
people of New Zealand. It will be the sixth time that Bill English will come to a Budget,
magically find money for private schools and ma gically find money for tax cuts for the
rich, but not find money to deliver to New Z ealanders so that everyone gets a good start
in life.
14 May 2014 General Debate 17839
On this side of the House we have set the policy agenda. We have come out with
KiwiBuild. We have come out with NZ Power.  They will help get people into homes
and improve the cost of living. We have come  up with the Best Start policy, which will
genuinely give all New Zealanders a best st art. Sue Moroney has her bill for 26 weeks’
paid parental leave. Labour has led the policy agenda, and National has lagged behind.
Tomorrow National might try to come up with  something to mimic Labour’s policies,
but it will not go far enough. It will not deliver opportunity for all New Zealanders.
What I can promise New Zealanders today is that the first Budget of the Labour
Government next year will put people first. We will ensure that all New Zealanders get
a fair go by reforming mone tary policy and by ensuring th at everybody pays their fair
share with a tax policy where higher-income ea rners actually pay their tax and actually
pay their fair share, and where we have a cap ital gains tax that takes the speculators out
and gives first-home buyers a chance. That will be an economy where people come first,
not the wealthy few and the speculators over th ere. Tomorrow is an opportunity for this
Government, but it will be one more big Bill English fail.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: As we move into the Budget
tomorrow, I want to rise and congratulate the team at Radio New Zealand. You may ask
why I would start my speech with congratul ations to Radio New Zealand. Well, the
reason is that Radio New Zealand appeared  before the Commerce Committee last week
for its financial review. The chair and chief ex ecutive of that august institution reported
a significant turn-round in the business. They reported that staff morale was high, that
the funding was secure for 18 months, and that the opportunities for growth were
unprecedented. This is after 6 years of no baseline increase.
The response from the Opposition members to that improvement in Radio New
Zealand was revealing. They were simply incredulous. How could one of their favourite
organisations be in better shape after 6 years with no baseline increases? That
philosophy, that approach to businesses goes to the heart of why that side of the House
should never ever take the Treasury benches. Their total philosophy is that the only way
we can improve organisations is to spend more—to spend more. That is the only way to
get out of a hole. But Radio New Zealand is in good shape. It has transformed from an
inefficient bureaucracy to a modern, lean busin ess that has a very bright future. That is
the same thing that has occurred across the State sector with the policies of this National
Government. It is a fantastic way forward and it is a good entry to the Budget.
I want to talk about the Budget and, I guess, the policies, because that gives us the
opportunity to contrast quite different policie s as we get into the next few days. Most
particularly, I want to focus on Mr Cunli ffe’s approach to getting the unemployment
rate down. Right now, after a re cession and significant issues that this Government has
faced, the unemployment rate has reduced from  7.2 percent down to 6 percent. I predict
that over the next few months it will be in to the 5 percent range. Unemployment is
coming down, and it is coming down under the po licies of this Government. So let us
look. His goal is to bring unemployment down to 4 percent, but it is actually an
oxymoron—Labour policies and low unemployment. Here are just three policies where
we differ quite significantly.
The first is capital gains tax. The deputy leader of the Labour Party stood up just
before and said that the aim is to take mone y from the speculative industries and put it
into the productive sector of the economy. What Labour forgets to tell you is that it will
also tax small-business owners. It does not tell you that in the policy. Actually, if you
are a small-business owner, you have been in the business for 15 years, and your
business is worth under $200,000, then you may be exempted. But guess what! Most
businesses that employ lots of people are worth a lot more than $200,000, which means
they will be subject to a capital gains tax, as well. That is totally counter-productive to
17840 General Debate 14 May 2014
reducing unemployment. It is a disincentive for businesses to  go out and invest. That is
a fact.
Secondly, the other side of the House wants to  lift marginal tax rates. It wants to tax
the higher-income earners in this country—t he rainmakers, the people who go out and
employ people. It wants to tax them more . We do not. We want to bring taxes down
over time. Again, it is oxymoronic. Why woul d someone go out and work their guts out
when that side of the House wants to tax th em more? It wants to discourage them from
going out and employing people.
The last policy I want to reflect on as we lead into the Budget is around the
differences of our unemployment law. We introduced a wonderful policy—the 90-day
grievance-free period—which ha s promoted much employment in this country. That
side of the House wants to  axe it. It wants to get rid of it. What is that going to do? It is
going to discourage good employers from having a crack at a new employee and
encouraging them to come into their business.
So, just those three policies alone are totally c ounter-intuitive to Labour’s goal of
bringing unemployment down to 4 percent. On this side of the House we back
businesses. We are going to have a strong Budget that brings unemployment down. We
are going to be back in surplus. It is going to be a fantastic Budget, and I am going to be
proud to be part of the party that presents it.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: I love New Zealand. I st ood for Parliament for
the Green Party because I am passionate ab out finding solutions to the long-term
problems we face. There is no question that we are facing some pretty big challenges.
We heard from Dr Kennedy Graham earlier about the clear and present danger caused
by human-caused climate change. This is not a subject that is up for debate. We know it
is happening, and we know it is caused by us and our use of fossil fuels and our
deforestation. We have no choice—either we change what we are doing or nature will
change what we are doing for us. But we can change what we are doing and be better
off.
The National Government does not seem to beli eve that this is possible. It wants us
to keep doing more of the same—the things that will make climate change worse, that
pollute our rivers, that threaten our beach es, and that increase the gap between the
wealthy and the poor. National says that is just reality. The reality is we cannot afford to
keep doing more of the same thing in the long term. The reality is that we have fantastic
opportunities to green our econom y, which will create jobs and make New Zealand an
even better place to live. That is what the Green Party is here for.
The National Party would have New Zealande rs believe that the Greens are against
jobs. Nothing could be further from the trut h. We want high-wage jobs in a cleantech
economy. There is a report from Pricewater houseCoopers I would like to quote: “The
potential economic gains from low carbon development are too significant to be
ignored. … with the right policies, the clean technology sector in New Zealand could be
worth between NZ$7.5 billion and NZ$22 billion to the economy by 2015.” So how do
we do this? How do we decouple economic pr osperity from resource depletion and
fossil fuel use? We need the right policie s. We need to remove the barriers to
investment in clean technology. That is w hy our co-leader Russel Norman yesterday
announced the policy initiative cal led the Green Investment Bank. This is just the first
of a suite of positive initiatives we will be announcing in the run-up to the election in
order to get New Zealand on the right track—that is, creat ing good jobs in a high-tech,
low-carbon economy.
What is the Green Investment Bank? It is  Government-owned, but it is a for-profit
investment bank that will specialise in projects that increase sustaina bility. It will cost
the Government about $120 million over 3 years to set up. We can fund that by raising
14 May 2014 General Debate 17841
our royalties on oil and mining up to international averages. It will be financially self-
sustaining and it will earn good returns. Li ke the Superannuation Fund, it will be
entirely independent of the Government. This  is not a new or radical idea. Like most
Green Party policies, it has been done successf ully overseas. The oldest example is in
Germany. The State-owned, self-financing bank there has grown to be one of the most
successful investment banks in  the world, investing $73 bill ion in projects worldwide,
one-third of which have an environmenta l or climate protection dimension. Green
investment banks can be found in  Japan, Malaysia, and three of  the larger states in the
United States, including California and New York, and the Conservative Government in
the United Kingdom recently established a green investment bank there.
The Green Investment Bank is a perfect example of an opportunity for New Zealand
to create smart, green jobs that will benefit us  all in the long term . It is proven, it is
practical, it is forward-looking, and it deals wi th the reality of climate change and our
need to transition to a low-carbon economy. It is in sharp contrast to the National
Government’s strategy of doing more of the same—more mining, more oil drilling,
more motorways, more traffic, more da iry cows, and more ra w logs—leaving us
completely vulnerable to external shocks, to  rising oil prices, and to high costs for the
transportation system that we have right now. We are vulnerable to the challenge of
climate change and rising oil prices, and we have the opportunity to reduce that
vulnerability and leave all New Zealanders better off.
We love New Zealand. The Green Party is here to look af ter our precious
environment and to ensure that all of our  people have great opportunities for good jobs
well into the long term, well into the future. Thank you.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I am very excited that
tomorrow our superb Minister of Finance, the Hon Bill English, will be delivering his
sixth Budget under this National Government. It  will provide momentum to keep this
country moving forward and will stand in stark contrast to our poor cousins across the
Tasman, who have had to face harsh auster ity measures and heavy cutbacks in the
investment on their public serv ices. The reason that the Australian Government is in
such a poor state and that its finances are sliding downhill is very, very simple—that is,
years of Labor and Greens misrule. The La bour and Green parties here in New Zealand
similarly offer no real substance, no real alternative. They can only sling mud.
I am sure that the New Zealand public will welcome this sensible, sound, and stable
National Government taking steps to lock in the very hard-w on progress that the
households, businesses, and, in fact, all ha rd-working New Zealanders are achieving.
The public also want to see this Government ’s accounts back in surplus, back in the
black, instead of the decade of deficits that was the inheritance of this Government from
the previous Labour one. We are starting to  see the pay-off from National’s good work.
Good GDP growth rates have meant that 84,000 new jobs ha ve been created in the
economy and real wages are rising. And the futu re is brighter yet. Here in Wellington,
in the home of the core public services, th ings are going well. Unlike the Opposition, I
do not disparage our hard-working public servants who are i nnovative in finding new
ways to deliver on improving serv ices to the public whilst operating in an environment
of constrained spending.
Obviously, the lion’s share of new meas ures will be announced in the Budget
tomorrow, but there have been a few announcem ents already made that I would like to
refer to. I support any message that helps grow New Zealand’s exports of innovative
products and services. Wellington is a creative hub for New Zealand, be it movie
making, software design, or even our craft beer  industry. So I am delighted that as part
of the Business Growth Agenda the Prim e Minister and Mini ster Groser have
announced an extra $69 million over 4 years fo r New Zealand Trade and Enterprise to
17842 General Debate 14 May 2014
boost New Zealand’s trade support teams in China, South America, and the Middle
East. Trade and Enterprise, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and those other
agencies that support New Zealand firms selling their products offshore deserve our
congratulations and our thanks for the incr eases in trade that they have achieved
alongside those hard-working people in the private sector over the past few years. As an
ex - Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trad e employee who had a couple of postings to
the Middle East, I think it is absolutely fant astic that the Government is investing in
giving even more support to exporters in these challenging but highly lucrative markets.
I also welcome an excellent measure that  supports some of the most dedicated
servants of State who have often taken huge risks to safeguard our country—that is, the
veterans of the armed forces. Today’s announcement by Minister Woodhouse of a $60
million investment in veterans support serv ices is simply wonderful, in my view.
Extending the veterans pension to every singl e one of those who have served, once they
reach 65 years of age, is the right thing to do. An extra 16,000 veterans will be
recognised for their service to  the country. I say to Labour members opposite that it is
an utter disgrace that they are considering ra ising the age of eligibility for the veterans
pension to 67 years of age. There are memb ers over there who know that that is the
wrong thing to do, and they should be standing up to their leader on that particular issue
for those who have sacrificed to ensure our freedoms.
Another announcement that I particularly welcome is the extra $10.4 million over 2
years to support front-line sexual violence services. Fo r those members who do not
think that such issues as hu man trafficking are a problem in  our country, I would invite
them to read this paper by Shimal Sataiya and Mark Calderwood of Waikato University:
Critical Analysis of Child Trafficking in New Zealand. We need to take urgent action on
this scourge. The situation in Nigeria with Boko Haram is not unique to that area. There
are issues here in New Zealand. We are investi ng in that area. That is the right thing to
do. I welcome that initiative, as will New Zealanders tomorrow. Thank you.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: On the eve of the Budget I wish we had a Labour
Government, and at the next Budget we will.  We will be looking at opportunity for all
New Zealanders. It will be a Budget that will ensure all Ne w Zealanders can participate
to their full potential. But that is not what New Zealand looks like at the moment. On
any measure, inequality is increasing under this National Government. I find it
fascinating to see how sensitive members on the other side are on this issue, because
they know this to be true. In question tim e today we saw them all ducking and diving.
They do not believe that figure and they do not agree with that figure. Even figures from
entirely reputable sources—they do not agree with those figures. Well, not only are they
out of touch; they are actually trying to hide the facts.
I just want to note that on many reputable  figures, including on OECD measures, the
evidence is quite clear: New Zealand has high income inequality. In fact, Bill English
seemed to say, as a matter of some pride, that even though we are one of the worst for
inequality in the OECD, we are stable at  that position. Well, hello, that is not good
enough. We want to do much, much better and we want New Zealand to go back to
being a more equal country, a country where every New Zealander can get ahead, where
every child has opportunity. The Prime Minist er does not even agree with the figures
confirmed by Treasury that 285,000 children ar e living in poverty, which is actually
45,000 more than when National took office. Of  course, the Salvation Army scored the
National Government a D—a D—on that particul ar measure. So those figures are there
for everybody to see.
I want to talk about Auckland. I am a proud Aucklander. I am based in the
Maungakiekie electorate, and we have seen  reports that under National there are two
Aucklands. In fact, the New Zealand Herald talked about a tale of two cities. It was not
14 May 2014 General Debate 17843
talking about Charles Dickens’ book A Tale of Two Cities , although there may be some
parallels there, one of the main themes in  that book being about social justice. That
book talked about two cities: London and Paris. In this case we are talking about within
Auckland. The article compared people living in the eastern suburbs—in the Ōrākei
area, Mission Bay, and St Heliers, where incomes were up signi ficantly—with those
living in M āngere and Ōtāhuhu, where incomes have actually fallen. The net effect of
that, according to the Salvation Army, is something like a 19 percent drop for people
already on a low income, and those people have  got an even worse standard of living.
That is all under this National Governme nt and that is putting communities under
significant stress.
I want to reflect on the fact  that in the Maunga kiekie electorate, where I work, I can
see those inequalities, and I am not the onl y one. If the Government thinks that New
Zealanders are not seeing this, it is very wrong on that matter. New Zealanders do see it.
There was a survey quoted earlier where 75 pe rcent of New Zealanders believed that
inequality was increasing. Of course, Bill English said: “Well, it doesn’t matter what
they think. It’s just not right.” Well, actually, they see it with their own eyes. They see it
in terms of family members struggling. They see it in terms of people unable to put food
on the table. They see it in terms of their own children unable to even contemplate
buying a house. They see it with loan sharks  proliferating all around the city of
Auckland. Forty-six percent of workers saw no increase in their pay rate in the 12
months to March and yet costs keep going up. That is something the Government wants
to try to deny but those figures are correct : 46 percent saw no increase. We need to
focus on jobs and we need to focus on lif ting wages, and that will happen under a
Labour Government.
Housing is the other big issue. Homeowne rship is plummeting, and that is most
pronounced in Auckland. I just want to remi nd people about the member of Parliament
for Maungakiekie, the Hon Peseta Sam Lotu-Ii ga. He said that there were 1,100 homes
under $500,000 in Maungakiekie and that $13 0,000 as a deposit was not out of reach.
That is how out of touch th e National Government is. T hose figures are clearly not
correct. Those assertions are not correct. H ousing is a significant problem. We have
senior citizens worried about be ing chucked out of their houses.  I have talked to people
with heart problems and with cancer who ar e being ripped out of  their Housing New
Zealand properties as we speak. There is  a shortage of housing throughout that
electorate. Thank you.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
speak in this general debate today. I begin by congratulating our Prime Minister and our
Minister of Finance on their leadersh ip in managing the New Zealand economy
outstandingly. We in the National Party we re handed over an economy that was in a
dismal state, a country where most of the skilled youth were inc lined to migrate to
Australia because they could not see a future  for themselves in their own country. Not
only was our talented and skilled labour fo rce migrating out of New Zealand, we were
failing to attract skilled migrants to our shores.
It is with great pride today that each of  us in the National Party can share with you
and with all New Zealanders that due to the strong leader ship provided by the Prime
Minister, John Key, and the pragmatic approach taken by our finance Minister, Bill
English, they have turned New Zealand into  what not too long a go was described as,
and as noted by an economist from HSBC, the rock star economy.
In case anyone in the Opposition feels that th is was an easy task, let me be blunt and
say that it took a lot of hard work in the past almost 6 years, to undo the damage that
was done by our Opposition colleagues when they were in Government. It is because of
17844 General Debate 14 May 2014
this hard work that we are optimistic that our economy is on the right track to reach our
goal of a Budget surplus this year.
Our migrant community has played an activ e role in the succe ss of our economy. At
the start of my speech I alluded to Kiwi s leaving the shores of New Zealand for
Australia because, in their opinion, Aust ralia can provide a better lifestyle. The
Australian Government yesterday presente d its Budget for 2014-15, and from what any
common person can understand, the Government in Australia has to address a number
of challenges through that B udget. The challenges posed to  the Australian economy are
without doubt due to the r eckless spending by the previous  Australian Labor-Green
coalition Government. A recent study by Deutsc he Bank says that Australia is one of
the most expensive countries in the world. Th e Australian Prime Minister has said that
the Budget presented by the finance Mini ster is a problem-solving Budget because
Australia has very serious problems of debt and deficit stretching as far as the eye can
see, but that it is also a nation-building Budget.
Therefore, I urge all New Zealanders to seriously consider the pragmatic work done
by the National Party Government in the past 6 years and start to imagine the negative
consequences that a Labour-Green Government  can have on the 6 years of hard work
done by the National Government. In India ther e is a saying “Jitne chadar ho utne peer
phelana.”, which means to live within one ’s own means. We in the National Party
believe in living within our own means. By  comparison, all other Opposition colleagues
do not share the same thought and have a sh ared spending plan, like the recent opening
of the Green Investment Bank. The question they  have to ask themselves is, of course:
where is the money coming from?
Here I would like to share that the migran ts who come over here have got dreams to
be successful. I would like to give an exampl e. Some of my fellow Indians started as
taxi drivers, but today I see a lot of th em are progressing. They are going into the
trucking business, and here I would like to quote the latest survey by the ANZ Heavy
Traffic Index. The index, which reflects our  truck movement on 11 roads, selected
because they have historically given good indications of economic activities at the time,
rose 0.5 percent just in the last month. To me, this is a very encourag ing statistic as this
means that despite—

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise
and speak in the Committee stage of the F ood Bill, having sat thr ough endless hours in
the Primary Production Committee listening to submissions on the formation of, and
amendments to, this bill. I think it is  probably worth noting at the beginning the
chronology of the bill. The bi ll was first introduced into  the House on 26 May 2010, it
had its first reading on 27 July 2010, and was reported on by the Primary Production
Committee on 16 December 2010. On 2 July 2013 it was returned to the Primary
Production Committee for a second round, having been delayed and then revisited as a
result of the whey protein concentrate sc are. The select committee had a couple of
substantial goes at amending the original bi ll and then the Supplementary Order Paper
that subsequently followed as a result of that.
The points that were made by the sele ct committee are well covered in the
commentary that the select committee reported back to the House, and it is worth
14 May 2014 Food Bill 17845
touching on a couple of those. To the pur pose of the bill we recommended adding
clause 4(ba) to make it clear th at one of the primary purposes of the bill is to maintain
New Zealand’s reputation as a producer and ex porter of safe and suitable food. I think
that cuts right to the nub of what this bill is about, at one end of it, and that is that New
Zealand is an export nation of protei n-based food—and other types of food, but
predominantly protein-based food—which have the opportunity, I guess, within them to
carry all sorts of poten tial dangers from a food safety point of view. To have a robust
legislative framework around controls and Government responses to those types of risks
from a reputational point of view is an  essential ingredient  to New Zealand’s
economy—more than I think most people real ise, given that something like 72 to 73
percent of all export earnings from New Z ealand come from our primary sector. That
was a major consideration in the deliberations on this bill.
At the other end of the spectrum, of course, you have the small fund-raising
committees, etc., such as Lions, Rotary clubs , marae, school calf days, those kinds of
things, where there was a pretty heavy-ha nded, bureaucratic approach, and so it was
decided that there must be a better way. Through, like I say, a long process we believe
that we have arrived at a point where we ha ve achieved that. I l ook forward to debating
various parts of this bill as it moves through the Committee.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
speak in this Committee stage of the Food B ill. I believe I may have just nipped ahead
of my colleague Mr O’Connor. I will start this off.
I am pleased to be speaking in this Committ ee stage. This is a significant piece of
legislation. As we know, it has had many year s in development, going all the way back
to when Labour was in Government. It is a very important piece of legislation because
we need a modern, risk-based food safety re gime. As we are on Part 1, I would like to
start my contribution right at the very start,  where clause 3(1) says: “This Act replaces
the Food Act 1981.” That is a ve ry welcome provision becaus e that is a very outdated
piece of legislation—30-plus years old—and it has caused a host of difficulties for
many small businesses and terri torial authorities right ac ross the country over a long
period of time. It is very welcome that we will be putting this bill through so that we can
see the repeal of that particular piece of legislation.
Just to give you an example, there are ma ny small businesses across the country that
have been stymied at times by overly bureaucra tic territorial authorities that have been
trying to fit the archaic piece of legisla tion, the Food Act 1981, to the operations of
modern food vendors and modern purveyors of ka i, of food. To give you an example,
we have had a host of some really bizarre  situations—for instance, a cafe owner in
Tūrangi, Ms Upston’s great electorate. Unfortuna tely, the district c ouncil there insisted
that with the installation of a new toasted-sandwich maker, that cafe had to install a
commercial-grade extractor that cost mo re than $7,000—just because the cafe operator
wanted to have a toasted-sandwich maker. Fo rtunately, these absolutely really bizarre
draconian measures that have been placed on cafe owners are eliminated through the
introduction of this legislation.
There are other examples, such as the kuias , the old ladies, up in the far north who
made strawberry jam and sold it at the local Kerikeri hospice charity shop. Those lovely
dear ladies found that they had to produce their jam in a commercial kitchen, so they
were technically contravening the law. Again, these really bizarre outcomes stymied the
entrepreneurial spirit and the generosity of these small businesses.
There are other examples of territorial aut horities really struggling with the one-size-
fits-all prescriptive approach  of the Food Act 1981, because, as we know, back in the
early 1980s it was far different from what we have today. I think it was simpler. We did
have fish and chips and fast food, but we  did not have things like, I guess, online
17846 Food Bill 14 May 2014
purchases of food. The industr ial techniques of producing fo od have really come on in
leaps and bounds over that period of time. Th erefore, the legislat ion of 1981 is really
out of date, and it is a very welcome move under this legislation that we will finally say
goodbye not only to that Act bu t also to the prescriptive  regulations that were
promulgated under that piece of legislation, because those regulations added to the
complexity and the cost and the bizarre out comes for small-business owners. What we
are getting under this piece of legislation is a much more suitable piece of legislation
that fits all types of food businesses, fr om the small coffee cart and the small cottage-
industry jam-maker right through to the big industrial processes and, indeed, exporters.
It is a well-thought-through piece of legisl ation, and can I commend all of the
officials who have spent many years on this  and also, especially, members of the
Primary Production Committee, who have give n it very close consideration and made
some very good improvements, especially Supplementary Order Paper 278 from the
Minister for Food Safety. Things like the good old Kiwiana sausage sizzle have been
given due recognition that they  do not need overly bureaucra tic sorts of food standards
and other compliance measures placed over th e top of them. So there are some real
common-sense amendments that have been made to get the bill to this Committee stage.
But there is one glaring omission in this bi ll in Part 1. Thankfully, my colleague the
Hon Damien O’Connor has proposed a very sensible amendment in Supplementary
Order Paper 440 that there be country-of-origin  labelling included in  clause 4. That is
very important because we on this side of the Chamber and many other parties here—
except for Peter Dunne, whom this amendment really rests on—believe that Kiwis have
the right to know the origin of  the food that they consume and that they purchase. It
should be implemented through this Supplementary Order Paper. I encourage the
members of this Committee to take the opportunity to make this very sensible
improvement to Part 1 so that we do add that element of, as Mr O’Connor calls it,
COOL—to adopt the acronym for country-of-or igin labelling. I am not really getting
any jokes out of this. We need to adopt the cool. We need some coolness. We need to
put some cool into the country-of-origin labelling in clause 4.
I would like to go back to my favourit e example, which is the good old Kiwi
sausage, the banger, and bacon. Very few Kiwis know that the majority of the pork that
is consumed in this country actually come s all the way from Canada, North America.
Should there be country-of-origin labelling, I think people will be a bit more thoughtful
in terms of the origin of their pork, of their food, and where it comes from. They do
have a right to know. So that is one sensib le amendment that I do recommend in my
contribution on this first part. Thank you.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : I have to
apologise to my colleague Rino Tirikatene, whom I left out in the lurch a little bit. I was
trying to escape a meeting.
We welcome the Food Bill into the Committ ee. It has been a long time coming. In
debating Part 1 of the bill I would like to, firstly, acknowledge some of the officials
there, many of whom have been around for as long as this bill has and as long as I have,
which is quite some time. We hope that th e ageing of the bill, like a good wine, has
improved it. A number of Ministers for Food Safety have overseen it, and I welcome the
current Minister’s comments on a number of the provisions.
In Part 1 of the bill we have, as rightfully it should be, the purpose of the bill. I have,
as my colleague noted, proposed an amen dment on Supplementary Order Paper 440,
which we believe is essential to finish off what is, essentia lly, a very good bill,
following almost 10 years, I guess, of c onsideration of assessment by the Primary
Production Committee on, indeed, a couple of occasions and, as I say, oversight and
14 May 2014 Food Bill 17847
input from people up and down this country  on at least two occasions and other
opportunities through consultation with officials.
If I can go to the purpose of the bill, it is, indeed, an amalgam of pieces of legislation
that have been around for a while. We are atte mpting to align those pieces of legislation
to give better effect to the purpose of producing safe food, maintaining New Zealand’s
reputation, and ensuring that consumers get a good deal from a country that we say—
and I think we can rightfully say—is one of the best producers of food in the world, bar
none.
The purpose of the bill, and I can read out cl ause 4, is to: “(a) restate and reform the
law relating to how persons trade in food; a nd (b) achieve the safety and suitability of
food for sale; and (ba) maintain confidence in New Zealand’s food safety regime”. That
was an amendment put up by the Primar y Production Committee to emphasise the
reality that the confidence th at the public have in the le gislation around food should not
be in question, and that this is  not a partisan piece of legi slation. It has been endorsed,
and I hope it will be, by all parties across the House beca use we have attempted to
achieve the very best outcome. The inclusi on of that subclause in the purpose clause,
that is, to maintain the confidence in New Zealand’s food safety regime, was an
important addition.
The next subclause is to “(c) provide for risk-based measures that—(i) minimise and
manage risks to public health; and (ii) protect and promote public health.” That is a very
important part and objective of this piece of  legislation. The fourth one is to “(d)
provide certainty for food businesses in relation to how the requirements of this Act will
affect their activities;”
We have, up and down this country—from th e very largest producers of food to the
very smallest and most innovative and creativ e, at times—people who, in classic Kiwi
style, get out, look around them, see what  opportunities there are and often through
biological production systems, be it through grapes or honey and bees or through new
fruit varieties, come up with a new food that they want to manufacture, or, indeed, to
just sell in its raw form. This piece of legisl ation has to give them certainty so that the
time and the money that they might invest  in that production system is supported
through legislation, through good regulations, and through a system that is going to give
them the opportunity to develop that further.
If I can use the example, going back some time, of kiwifruit, the humble Chinese
gooseberry, which was grown on a few farms and in a few gardens around the place and
has now become a billion-dollar industry because the regulations were sound, and
because of the ability for those growers to develop the intellectual property, the
varieties, and to get out ther e and develop the systems of handling, of storage, and of
sale—the legislation had to  support that development through the years. We are
upgrading the legislation to modernise it and to make it fit for purpose.
The next thing here is subclause (d), to “provide certainty for food businesses”, and
then moving on to clause 4(e), which is to “require persons who tr ade in food to take
responsibility for the safety a nd suitability of that food.” [ Interruption] I acknowledge
the Minister, and I would welcome responses.
This is, I guess, an area where responsibil ity is placed back on to the people in the
food sector themselves. The risk-based system  that we are proposing puts trust in them
to do what they say they are going to do in ad ministering the regime at whatever level.
The people who are taking responsibility are those who are trading in food and it is
about ensuring that they deliver to their cons umers, to their customers, food that is not
too old, does not have contaminants in it, or does not have food safety issues that might
harm them in any way. The regime that we ha ve is a very stringent risk-based system
for those from the very top—Fonterra and the big producers—down to the person
17848 Food Bill 14 May 2014
selling sausages for the sausage sizzle. Ther e are different requirements that ultimately
depend upon the individuals i nvolved, or the companies in volved, to implement what
they say they will do. The officials can neve r be there every moment of every day. I
think we are lucky to be in a country that has people of integrity, systems of integrity,
and regulations that are generally sound and sensible. We should be  able to trust the
systems once this legislation passes.
All those objectives, we sa y, are sound, but there is one missing, and I know I have
had discussions with the Minister—hopefully, she has seen the light of day to come and
support us—on mandatory country-of-origin labelling, informing the consumers who
buy the food where the food was produced and manufactured. We say that it is a core
right of any consumer to know where the f ood they are eating has come from. We are
part of a trans-Tasman arrangement, the Food Standards Australia New Zealand
authority, which says that we share with Australia the same regime for risk-based
systems, for food safety, and for labelling. So using CER and the transfer of goods
either side of the Tasman aligns and makes that system more simple.
But New Zealand sought an exemption from  those trans-Tasman  regulations that
allows us to not have country-of-origin la belling. For a country so dependent upon food
production for our survival and our prosperit y, it is absolutely bizarre that we do not
have country-of-origin labelling—something that identifies clearly the food produced in
this country under regulation that would al low consumers to know whether that food
was produced and manufactured in New Zealand or whether it was produced
somewhere else in the world.
I am proposing Supplementary Order Paper 440 and an amendment that would add to
the purpose clause in the bill a requirement  to introduce country -of-origin labelling
requirements in accordance with the Austra lia - New Zealand food standards code. The
exemption that we have—and the Minister mi ght say “Oh, it’s not appropriate to have
this in the bill.” That is absolutely wrong. It  is appropriate that we have in the purpose
of this bill a requirement to align ourselves with the agreed regulations that are currently
in place on both sides of the Tasman. So I we lcome the Minister’s response as to why
the National Party and its two coalition pa rtners, Peter Dunne a nd Mr Banks, are not
supporting something that the vast majority of the public expects.
Country-of origin labelling is taking plac e in some areas through a voluntary code,
but it is not mandatory and, in fact, ther e are many occasions when consumers are
confused as to where the food they are pur chasing is grown and manufactured. We will
be putting to the Committee this amendment to  the purpose in Part 1 of the bill, and I
hope that the Government can see the wis dom in supporting that for the good of the
consumers and for their right to have information and knowledge about the food that
they are going to consume.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to take this call
in the Committee of the whole House stage. Can I start by acknowledging that this is, I
think, a great day for New Zealand. It has been over 10 years in the making. There have
been many officials in a number of administra tions who have worked on this Food Bill.
I want to acknowledge what I acknowledged in the second readi ng. There have been
several Ministers. I also want to acknowledge the huge amount of work across this
House that has gone into making this bill be tter. I acknowledge also  that this bill is
supported by the Labour Party, the Green Party, United Future , the ACT Party, I
believe, and I think Brendan Horan is suppor ting it too. I think when we come to the
purpose of this bill, we can see why it has su ch cross-party support. It has cross-party
support because at the heart of this bill is, actually, our nation’s economy. If we do not
get food safety right, then all of us are much poorer and our quality of life is poorer.
14 May 2014 Food Bill 17849
What this bill does is two things. The first is that it says we are actually going to base
our food law on the risk of food and not build ings. We are on the cu sp of replacing the
30-year-old statute, which will actually ensure  that food safety is based on the risk of
food, not buildings and an outdated un-modern  statute. The second key thing that has
actually been at the heart of much of what I think was genuine concern about this statute
is allowing New Zealanders to do what they have always done and to not have
compliance costs on so many small businesses. That is why I am very pleased that the
Primary Production Committee gave a lot of at tention to understanding the impact on
small businesses. This is a sliding scale regi me. The advice that I have had is that $40
million in compliance costs will go out the wind ow with this bill. The third thing, as we
saw, was the sausage sizzle issue. That was an issue very dear to the heart of New
Zealanders. I think the select committee has really improved the bill to ensure that those
community groups that are fund-raising can go on and do what they have always done. I
really think this is a great bill from the pe rspective that not only is  it going to help so
many small businesses across New Zealand have  consistency in terms of food safety
regulation but also it is going to reduce comp liance costs and it is going to enable New
Zealanders to do what they have always done.
There are a couple of Supplementary Order Pa pers, and I just want  to address both
Supplementary Order Paper 440, which Da mien O’Connor put forward, and also
Steffan Browning’s variation within the H ouse, Supplementary Order Paper 449. From
our perspective, New Zealand has country of origin labelling. It is voluntary. I have
actually been doing some work to look at wh at that coverage is. What I can tell the
Committee is that the advice that I have ha d is that, in terms of single-ingredient
country of origin labelling—a nd I want to talk about th e difference in a second—we
estimate about 70 percent of coverage happens in terms of country of origin labelling
for single ingredients. That is, about 70 perc ent of fruit, vegetabl es, and meat in our
supermarkets have country of  origin labelling. So the qu estion is twofold. How do we,
possibly, encourage more of that? Secondly, is it appropriate in this statute to pass a law
that requires mandatory country of origin labelling?
The first point I want to make—and I think this is very relevant for the Opposition—
is that some of the advice I have had is that we w ould actually be breaching the
Australia - New Zealand food treaty if we pa ssed this law. We have set up a regime
where we have been really clear—and Mr O’Connor, you have mentioned in your
speech—that we develop standards with Australia. Yes, they have developed a standard
in this area, but we absolutely have the ab ility to adopt country of origin labelling
through that process that we have agreed to  with Australia. To pass a law via statute
rather than the code is actually not the process that we agreed to with Australia. From
my perspective, it is not appropriate in this bill.
However, I want to raise a couple of i ssues generally around country of origin
labelling. The other point I wa nt to make to the Oppositio n is that they may not be
aware but Australia has just launched an inqui ry into country of origin labelling. The
advice that I have had is that  part of what the committee ch airing that inquiry said in
Australia is that there is widespread confusion there around the differences in
terminology between “made in Australia”, “product of Australia ”, and “made from
Australian”. What this is about is actually recognising that although it may be relatively
easy to deal with single ingred ient country of origin label ling, when you are asking and
trying to pass a law for when you may have 10 to 12 different ingredients, the reality, as
I think Australia is find ing, is one, the complexity of tryi ng to then label the source of
all of those products; two, the cost to business to be able  to do that; and, then, three—
and this is why I think Australia has la unched this inquiry—how meaningful it is
actually to consumers if you have got a whole lot of different sources of ingredients.
17850 Food Bill 14 May 2014
I want to finish that issue by saying that  the Government does at this point support
voluntary country of origin labelling. We do think, from the advice that I have had—but
I am going to do a bit more work on it—that we have got quite a lot of take up around
single-ingredient country of origin labelli ng, but in terms of comprehensive country of
origin labelling I would enc ourage the Opposition to look at the fact that Australia is
actually launching an inquiry into this i ssue, because, I think, of the confusion, the
complexity, and the cost.
Again, I want to acknowledge why we are here. We are here, in part, to reduce
compliance costs to businesses. We are here to ensure there is much greater alignment
across the country in te rms of food safety laws. In term s of the purpose of the bill, as
well, we are here to ensure that New Z ealanders can go on and do what they have
always done. I think, as well, we are also here—and I want to acknowledge the select
committee and its patience on this issue—because  we had a major food safety incident
last year. I think what that incident outlined for us was, one, the importance of food
safety to New Zealand and our economy, and, secondly, the need to ensure that we not
only get our primary legislation right but also do whatever we can to reduce complexity
in some of those tertiary instruments. I think this is a great bill. It is going to be great for
New Zealand. I want to acknow ledge again, although we may ha ve a few differences in
terms of some of the Supplementary Orde r Papers, the incredib le support that has
happened across the Committee to make this bill better. Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I am pleased to rise on behalf of New Zealand
First to take a call in this Committee of th e whole House as we continue to debate the
Food Bill. I would just like to say, first o ff, following on from the Minister for Food
Safety, that we will be supporting Suppl ementary Order Paper 440 in the name of
Damien O’Connor and also Supplementary Order Paper 449 in the name of Steffan
Browning, which is very similar and complement ary. In this part of our deliberations I
want to focus on some of the perhaps less glam orous aspects of the bi ll. In any piece of
legislation there will be much that is mundane yet none the less necessary. Not every
subclause or annotated paragraph will set th e world on fire, but each of them provides
an essential cog in the machinery of law. With that in mind, the first thing I want to look
at is Part 1, clause 8, which relates to the meaning of food.
To an independent observer, this may appear to be a somewhat unnecessary
consideration. The average citizen, I might  posit, could perhaps be forgiven for
presuming that the definition of “food” was a fairly straightforw ard affair: if you eat
something, it is food. Not so in the eyes of the law. The proof of that particular pudding
is in Part 1, clause 8, “Meaning of food”. In  this bill clause 8( 1) states: “unless the
context otherwise requires, food—(a) means anything that is used, capable of being
used, or represented as being for use, for human consumption (whether raw, prepared,
or partly prepared); and (b) includes—(i) s eeds, plants, or plant material intended for
human consumption, including seed s that are intended to be sprouted and consumed as
sprouts, but not other seeds, plants, or plant material intended for planting;”.
So a potato is food, but a seed spud is not. What is the difference between a spud and
a seed spud, one might ask. Well, a seed spud is a spud that has gone to seed. It may
have been grown especially with that purpose in mind. As  such, it could rightly be
classified as not being intended for human c onsumption. Equally, it may be an ordinary
spud originally intended for eating but that has somehow been overlooked—it may have
languished at the bottom of the bag, at the back of  the pantry, alone and forlorn in the
dark until it has thrown out a few of those pale, spindly shoots by which the life force of
the potato plant attempts to replicate itself. At that time the intention for it to become
the subject of human consumption is extinguis hed. Under the definition in the law as it
is enshrined in this bill, it is therefore no l onger food. That is not to say that such a spud
14 May 2014 Food Bill 17851
can be presumed to now be intended for planting. Such an accidental seed spud may
well find itself in the charge and care of a non-gardener, and it may very well come to
end its days in the compost bin or worse. But that is of no matter. The important point is
that it is no longer food in a le gal sense. This is an importa nt distinction, and one that
has to be made. I would venture to suggest to the House that this bill makes that
distinction rather well.
Food is also defined, under clause 8(1)(b), as “(ii) live animals intended for human
consumption at the place of purchase; a nd (iii) live animals intended for human
consumption that are sold in retail premises;”. I presume this refers primarily to such
comestibles as lobster, or perhaps live shellfish, but, equally, it could conceivably
include live chickens purchased for later preparation. Again, this is an important
consideration, because if the b ill did not contain a specific reference to the intention for
the live animal to be for human consumpti on, every pet shop in the country might find
itself in a very unenviable position. Once again, we see the tiny cogs of the great
machine performing their sterling servic e, mostly unseen and, presumably,
underappreciated, but, none the less, completely necessary.
The bill also provides, under the definition of the meaning of food, “(iv) any
ingredient or other constituent of any food or  drink, whether that ingredient or other
constituent is consumed or represented fo r consumption on its own by humans, or is
used in the preparation of, or mixed with  or added to, any f ood or drink; and (v)
anything that is or is intended to be mixed w ith or added to any food or drink; and (vi)
chewing gum, and any ingredient of chewing gum, and anything that is or is intended to
be mixed with or added to chewing gum;”. So chewing gum is food. This may come as
something of a surprise to members. It ha s come to pass that ge nerations of children
were right all along and their parents were wrong.
Chewing gum is food because Parliament, by its sovereign power and authority, has
decreed that it be so. Tobacco, however, is not food, and rightly  so. I think most
members, if not all, would agree that tob acco is not food—at least not food for humans.
This includes chewing tobacco. Unlike chewing gum, chewing tobacco may not
lawfully be food. It is not th e act of chewing, therefore, th at makes it food, or even the
non-swallowing of the substance in quest ion. Neither chewing gum nor chewing
tobacco are intended to be ingested, which ma y, in itself, seem somewhat incongruous
in terms of the ordinary pe rson’s perception of what food may be, given its intended
purpose. Rather, it is the letter of the law that determines th e relative foodness or non-
foodness of any particular substance.
In closing then, I will note that the bill also provides, in clause 8(1)(b)(vii), that food
is “anything that is declar ed by the Governor-General, by Order in Council made under
section 355, to be food for the purposes of this Act;”, and thus chewing gum may be
food but chewing tobacco may not, so must it be. These are splendid definitions and we
support them entirely, as we support this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: I am pleased to be able to speak in the
Committee of the whole House stage of the Food  Bill. Part 1 is pretty broad, and I think
we need to visit a few aspects of it. I will just reflect on the broa d level of agreement
that has been arrived at in terms of this bill across Parliament. But in saying that, that
does not mean that the Green Party is happy w ith all aspects of the bill—not just this
issue of country-of-origin labelling but othe r aspects as well. But we think there has
been a reasonable move to accept some of our  concerns and to address them. In time, I
would like to see further change to this bill. I referred to it last night that we actually do
need a truly independent New Zealand Food Sa fety Authority—not just the one that we
did have but something much more genuine ly independent. This bill goes a long way,
and it has been mentioned about the new pa rt in the purpose clause, inserted by new
17852 Food Bill 14 May 2014
clause 4 (ba), which is that the legisla tion will help “maintain confidence in New
Zealand’s food safety regime;”. That is all about external trade, and that is obviously
important, with agriculture being 54 percent of our export value. It is absolutely critical.
However, New Zealanders are being fed some  very, very poor food. This bill could
deal with that, but will not necessarily. The bill is full of mays and possibilities—the
Minister may do this, or the Ministry for Primary Industries may do that. But what we
actually need is some serious compliance. We ne ed to be looking at what is in our food,
who is measuring it, and how they are measurin g it. I have been involved in this issue
for many years—more than a decade—looking  at issues around pesticides in food,
genetically modified foods and how they are coming into the c ountry, and antibiotic
resistance and that. The bill can address them all, but so c ould the Food Act, and
successive Governments have failed New Zeal anders in the appli cation of legislation
and regulation to ensure the best food is goi ng to them, their children, and, in fact, their
unborn children as well. So I am looking fo rward to seeing very good and appropriate
application to ensure that this bill works well once it is passed.
There has been a fair bit of talk on country -of-origin labelling, and I am sure we are
going to address that several more times. I was just taking some notes when the
Minister for Food Safety was talking. We have  had some of these discussions before. I
do not think it is right that we rely on the jo int partnership, Minister . I have just been
reflecting on it a little bit ove r the last hour or so. The joint partnership with Australia
has some sense. We are a small country, Aust ralia is a much bigge r country, so let us
work together on food standard s. But what we are getting from them and what the
Minister is unfortunately being advised about are not necessarily good outcomes for
New Zealanders. I know that through and thr ough on genetic engineering. I am not sure
when I will do a speech on that through the course of what we are doing now, but I will.

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: Oh, dear!

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: And Ian McKelvie is waiting for that. I promise you, Ian,
I will give it to you.
